statement: Asset-backed securities backed by credit card receivables typically use a revolving structure.
explanation: Credit card receivables are short-dated, prepay quickly and have no fixed amortization schedule, so principal is returned in lump sums and the revolving structure suits them.
originalText: Credit card debt.

statement: Asset-backed securities backed by residential mortgages typically use a revolving structure.
explanation: Residential mortgages repay on an amortization schedule, so they typically use the amortizing (pass-through) structure rather than a revolving one.
originalText: Residential mortgage.
correction: Asset-backed securities backed by residential mortgages typically use an amortizing structure.

statement: Asset-backed securities backed by commercial mortgages typically use a revolving structure.
explanation: Commercial mortgages likewise amortize on a schedule, so they typically use the amortizing structure rather than a revolving one.
originalText: Commercial mortgage.
correction: Asset-backed securities backed by commercial mortgages typically use an amortizing structure.

statement: A specific provision on a loan classified as loss reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made, whereas the later write-off of that fully provided loan against the loan loss reserve leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged.
explanation: The provision is an income statement expense that also builds the loan loss reserve. Writing the loan off later removes equal amounts from gross loans and from the reserve, so nothing passes through the income statement again.
originalText: Last year’s provision reduced pre-tax earnings by USD 4 million; this year’s write-off leaves them unchanged.

statement: A specific provision leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged when it is made, and the later write-off of the fully provided loan reduces pre-tax earnings by the loan amount.
explanation: The provision is the expense that hits pre-tax earnings, because it is charged to the income statement. The write-off of a fully provided loan only cleans up the balance sheet and does not reduce earnings again.
originalText: Last year’s provision left pre-tax earnings unchanged; this year’s write-off reduces them by USD 4 million.
correction: A specific provision reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made, and the later write-off of the fully provided loan leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged.

changes.from: leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged when it is made
changes.to: reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made

changes.from: reduces pre-tax earnings by the loan amount

statement: Loan loss provisions, together with general loss reserves that normally count as Tier 2 capital and are not assigned to specific assets, form the basis of a bank's capacity to absorb losses.
explanation: GARP counts both specific provisions and the general reserve toward loss-absorbing capacity. The general reserve, held against losses not yet identified, is the part that normally counts as Tier 2 capital.
originalText: The provisions, together with the general reserve that normally counts as Tier 2 capital, form the basis of the capacity to absorb losses.

statement: Both specific provisions and general loss reserves are normally counted as Tier 2 capital, since both are loss allowances.
explanation: Only general loss reserves, held against presently unidentified losses, normally count as Tier 2 capital. Provisions against identified deterioration of particular assets do not.
originalText: Both the specific provisions and the general reserve are normally counted as Tier 2 capital, since both are loss allowances.

statement: Only specific provisions add to a bank's capacity to absorb losses, because a general loss reserve is not linked to any particular loan.
explanation: A general reserve is exactly the cushion for losses not yet tied to a particular loan, so it adds to loss-absorbing capacity together with the specific provisions.
originalText: Only the specific provisions add to the capacity to absorb losses, because the general reserve is not linked to any loan.

statement: IFRS 9 replaced the incurred loss model of IAS 39 with an expected loss model, so losses are provided for before any default occurs.
explanation: Under the incurred loss model a loan was impaired only after a loss event. IFRS 9 requires even performing loans to carry a 12-month expected loss, so provisions rise on adoption without new defaults.

statement: IFRS 9 kept the incurred loss model of IAS 39 but required the provision on every impaired loan to cover its lifetime losses.
explanation: IFRS 9 did not keep the incurred loss model. It replaced it with an expected loss model, under which even performing loans carry a provision.

statement: IFRS 9 requires every loan to carry a provision equal to its lifetime expected losses from the day it is granted.
explanation: Under IFRS 9 performing (stage 1) loans carry 12-month expected losses, and lifetime expected losses apply only after credit deterioration (stages 2 and 3). Lifetime losses from origination is the approach of the US CECL standard.
originalText: IFRS 9 required every loan to carry a provision equal to its lifetime expected losses from the day it is granted.

statement: IFRS 9 requires loan loss provisions to be counted as Tier 1 capital.
explanation: An accounting standard does not decide regulatory capital, and loan loss provisions are not Tier 1 capital.
originalText: IFRS 9 required provisions to be counted as Tier 1 capital, so the bank built them up to protect its capital ratios.

statement: Under IFRS 9 as described by GARP, a significant change in the credit environment moves a loan to stage 2 even if the borrower has no payment arrears.
explanation: GARP's stage 2 covers assets in arrears or where a significant change in the credit environment has occurred, for example when the original underwriting would now differ materially on price or terms. Waiting for arrears would recognise deterioration too late.
originalText: Stage 2, because a significant change in the credit environment moves a loan to stage 2 even without arrears.

statement: Under IFRS 9, only a missed payment can move a performing loan out of stage 1.
explanation: A missed payment is only one trigger. A significant change in the credit environment can also move a loan to stage 2 without arrears.
originalText: Stage 1, because only a missed payment can move a performing loan out of stage 1.

statement: Under IFRS 9, a current loan that would now be priced on significantly different terms is treated as nonperforming and placed in stage 3.
explanation: Stage 3 is for nonperforming assets. A fully current loan whose credit environment has changed significantly belongs in stage 2.
originalText: Stage 3, because a loan that would now be priced on different terms is treated as nonperforming.

statement: IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking estimate of expected losses, so provisions should reflect current and expected conditions and not past averages alone.
explanation: GARP states that IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking approach to loan loss estimation and provisioning. Historical data remain a legitimate input, but an estimate that ignores a worsening outlook is not forward-looking.
originalText: IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking estimate, so expected losses should reflect current and expected conditions, not past averages alone.

statement: IFRS 9 prohibits any use of historical loss data in estimating expected losses.
explanation: Historical loss data remain a legitimate input to expected loss estimates. IFRS 9 requires that they be combined with current and forward-looking information.
originalText: IFRS 9 prohibits any use of historical loss data, so the ten-year average must be replaced entirely by external credit ratings.

statement: Under IFRS 9, stage 1 loans require a provision for lifetime expected losses.
explanation: Stage 1 loans carry 12-month expected losses. Lifetime expected losses apply from stage 2.
originalText: Stage 1 loans require lifetime expected losses, so the horizon of the model is too short whatever data it uses.
correction: Under IFRS 9, stage 1 loans require a provision for 12-month expected losses.

statement: A supervisor assessing the effectiveness of workout procedures for problem loans looks at the unit's organization and staff, its attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and its average time to recovery.
explanation: GARP's assessment criteria cover the organization of the workout function, its performance through attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and the average time to recovery.
originalText: The unit’s organization and staff, its attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and its average time to recovery.

statement: The size of the loan loss reserve relative to the loan book, compared with peer banks, is a measure of the effectiveness of a bank's workout procedures.
explanation: The reserve ratio depends heavily on whether a bank retains or writes off loss assets, and on tax rules, so it does not measure workout effectiveness. Recovery rates, recovery time and the unit's organization do.
originalText: The size of the loan loss reserve relative to the loan book, compared with peer banks in the same country.

statement: Promptly writing loss assets off against the reserve, as in the US tradition, is more conservative than retaining them on the books, and a write-off does not mean that recovery on the asset is abandoned.
explanation: GARP calls the prompt write-off approach more conservative. Written-off loss assets are considered nonbankable but not necessarily nonrecoverable, so collection can continue.
originalText: Bank W’s approach is the more conservative, and writing a loss asset off does not mean that recovery on it is abandoned.

statement: Retaining loss assets on the books until all collection remedies are exhausted, as in the British tradition, is the more conservative approach because the larger loan loss reserve shows more is provided for each loss asset.
explanation: GARP calls the write-off approach more conservative. The larger reserve under retention only reflects loss assets that are still on the books, not more generous provisioning.
originalText: Bank R’s approach is the more conservative, because its larger loan loss reserve shows it provides more for each loss asset.

statement: A bank that writes a loss asset off gives up all collection efforts on it, since a write-off declares the asset to be unrecoverable.
explanation: Written-off assets are nonbankable but not necessarily nonrecoverable, so the bank can keep pursuing recovery after the write-off.
originalText: Bank W gives up all collection efforts on written-off assets, since a write-off declares the asset to be unrecoverable.

statement: The choice between retaining and writing off loss assets is set by IFRS 9 staging and so does not vary with the national tax treatment of provisions.
explanation: IFRS 9 staging governs expected loss provisioning, not this choice. GARP says the approach used in a country often depends on the taxation applied to provisions.
originalText: The choice between the approaches is set by IFRS 9 staging, so it does not vary with the national tax treatment of provisions.

statement: Using point-in-time rather than through-the-cycle PDs in an economic capital model makes capital more volatile and procyclical, because a borrower is less likely to keep the same rating under a point-in-time approach.
explanation: Capital calibrated to current conditions falls when the credit environment improves and rises when it deteriorates. The through-the-cycle approach reduces the volatility of economic capital because ratings are more stable.
originalText: Switching the economic capital model from TTC to PIT PDs would make capital more volatile and procyclical, because a borrower is less likely to keep the same rating under a PIT approach.

statement: Through-the-cycle ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, which makes them more volatile and more procyclical than point-in-time ratings.
explanation: Prompt updating and higher volatility describe point-in-time ratings. Through-the-cycle ratings are robust to short-term changes and updated less frequently.
originalText: Because TTC ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, they are the more volatile of the two philosophies and the more procyclical.
correction: Point-in-time ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, which makes them more volatile and more procyclical than through-the-cycle ratings.

statement: Through-the-cycle assessments are mainly employed in banks' internal rating systems, while point-in-time assessments are primarily of interest to the major credit rating agencies.
explanation: The roles are reversed. Point-in-time assessments are usually employed in banks' internal systems, while through-the-cycle assessments are primarily of interest to the major rating agencies.
originalText: TTC assessments are mainly employed in banks’ internal systems for short-term loans, while PIT assessments are primarily of interest for the major credit rating agencies.
correction: Point-in-time assessments are mainly employed in banks' internal rating systems, while through-the-cycle assessments are primarily of interest to the major credit rating agencies.

statement: Research shows that point-in-time assessments have unambiguously higher predictive power than through-the-cycle assessments, so point-in-time PDs should be used for every purpose, including economic capital.
explanation: Findings from existing research are mixed, so the choice depends on the scope of the analysis. Through-the-cycle PDs are the usual choice for economic capital.
originalText: Research shows that PIT assessments have unambiguously higher predictive power than TTC assessments, so the bank should use PIT PDs for every purpose, including economic capital.

statement: Rating agencies combine analytical and judgmental assessment of a wide range of inputs, gathered from proprietary databases, industry and market reports, and on-site meetings between agency analysts and the rated company's executives.
explanation: GARP describes agency ratings as combining analytical and judgmental approaches over many input data. The judgmental element also underlies the transparency criticism of ratings.
originalText: The rating will combine analytical and judgmental assessment of a wide range of inputs, gathered from proprietary databases, industry and market reports, and on-site meetings between the agency’s analysts and the company’s executives.

statement: A credit rating agency's rating is the output of an automated scoring model applied to the latest financial ratios, with no meeting with management and no qualitative factors.
explanation: That describes an automated internal credit score. Agency ratings combine analytical and judgmental approaches and include on-site meetings with the rated company's executives.
originalText: The rating will be the output of an automated scoring model applied to the latest financial ratios, so no meeting with management is involved and qualitative factors are excluded.

statement: Rating agencies publish one rating on a single scale for all horizons, since short-term and long-term credit risk are measured identically.
explanation: Agencies issue short-term ratings (typically one year) and medium- and long-term ratings, and may adopt different rating scales for different horizons.
originalText: The agency will publish one rating on a single scale for all horizons, since short-term and long-term credit risk are measured identically.

statement: Agency credit ratings are updated in real time as the rated company's share price moves, in the same way as a bank's point-in-time internal score.
explanation: Agency ratings are through-the-cycle in character and updated infrequently. Real-time movement is the point-in-time profile.
originalText: The rating will be updated in real time as the company’s share price moves, in the same way as a bank’s point-in-time internal score.

statement: Under Basel II and III, retail banks set aside a relatively small amount of capital, but must provide PD, LGD and EAD for clearly differentiated segments, segmented by credit score or an equivalent measure and by vintage.
explanation: Regulators view retail credit risk as relatively predictable and mortgages as safer, so retail attracts less capital than corporate lending. In return banks must supply PD, LGD and EAD statistics for clearly differentiated segments.
originalText: Retail banks set aside a relatively small amount of capital, but must provide PD, LGD and EAD for clearly differentiated segments, segmented by credit score or an equivalent measure and by vintage.

statement: Loans to small businesses can never be managed as retail exposures, because Basel's retail definition covers consumer loans only.
explanation: Small business loans can be treated as retail exposures if the total exposure to the borrower is below EUR 1 million.
originalText: Loans to small businesses can never be managed as retail exposures, because Basel’s retail definition covers consumer loans only.

statement: Retail exposures attract more capital than corporate loans of the same size, because retail losses are harder to predict.
explanation: Retail exposures attract relatively less capital than corporate loans under Basel, because retail credit risk is viewed as relatively predictable.
originalText: Retail exposures attract more capital than corporate loans of the same size, because the dark side makes retail losses harder to predict.

statement: Basel applies one capital formula to all retail exposures, so a mortgage and a credit card with the same PD carry the same capital requirement.
explanation: Basel treats three retail subsectors (residential mortgages, qualifying revolving credit and other retail) with three different formulas.
originalText: Basel applies one formula to all retail exposures, so a mortgage and a credit card with the same PD carry the same capital requirement.

statement: Keeping a single interest rate for all card applicants is likely to cause adverse selection, attracting mainly high-risk customers, and the extent of this may only become apparent when the economic climate deteriorates.
explanation: A one-price-fits-all policy in a competitive market attracts high-risk customers and discourages low-risk ones. This is the case for risk-based pricing by score band.

statement: The dark side of retail credit is mainly the risk that a loss on a single large customer exceeds its expected level in a downturn.
explanation: Large single-name exposures define corporate portfolios. The dark side of retail credit is an unforeseen systematic risk factor that influences the behaviour of many credits at once.
originalText: Because retail credit losses are relatively predictable, the dark side of retail credit is mainly the risk that a loss on a single large customer exceeds its expected level in a downturn.

statement: Because a retail portfolio behaves like a well-diversified portfolio, its expected loss can be priced in and the bank need not hold any capital against retail unexpected losses.
explanation: Expected loss can be priced in, but regulators still require a relatively small amount of risk capital for retail, because losses can rise to unexpected levels.

statement: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer's score band, the higher the interest rate charged.
explanation: Under tiered pricing the higher the score, the lower the price.
originalText: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer’s score band, the higher the interest rate charged, since high-scoring customers tend to use their credit lines more.
correction: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer's score band, the lower the interest rate charged.

changes.from: the higher the interest rate charged
changes.to: the lower the interest rate charged

statement: One prime cause of the dark side of retail credit risk is an operational issue in credit assessment that has a systematic effect on the whole consumer portfolio.
explanation: Consumer credit runs as a semiautomated decision process rather than a series of tailored decisions. An operational error in credit assessment can therefore affect the entire consumer portfolio at once.
originalText: An operational issue in credit assessment that has a systematic effect on the whole consumer portfolio.

statement: A scorecard is better the closer its cumulative accuracy profile lies to the 45-degree line, which is the benchmark a good model should track.
explanation: The 45-degree line is the random model. The closer a CAP curve sits to it, the worse the scorecard; a better scorecard lies closer to the perfect-model line.
originalText: Y is the better scorecard, because its CAP lies closer to the 45-degree line, which is the benchmark a good model should track.

statement: The accuracy ratios of two scorecards cannot be compared unless the bank's cutoff score is known.
explanation: A CAP is built from the whole population sorted by score and involves no cutoff, so the accuracy ratios of two scorecards on the same cohort are directly comparable.
originalText: The accuracy ratios of X and Y cannot be compared, because the bank’s cutoff score has not been given.

statement: A CAP curve that drifts towards the 45-degree line signals deteriorating scorecard performance, which can come from changes in the characteristics or the behaviour of the scored population.
explanation: A curve moving towards the diagonal means the scorecard ranks defaulters less well. GARP attributes such deterioration to changes in the population's characteristics and/or behaviour over time.
originalText: The drift signals deterioration, which can come from changes in the population’s characteristics or behaviour, and the switch to credit cards changes the target population enough to justify a new custom scorecard.

statement: Scorecard performance usually changes abruptly, so the CAP should be recomputed daily and the scorecard replaced the first time its accuracy ratio falls.
explanation: Scorecard performance tends to deteriorate gradually rather than abruptly, and GARP suggests monitoring it quarterly.

statement: A scorecard built for one product, such as auto loans, can be reused for a new product such as credit cards, because a scorecard's accuracy ratio depends only on the bank's own default rate.
explanation: A scorecard is built for a particular population. A new product brings a different population and calls for a new custom scorecard.
originalText: The auto-loan scorecard can be reused for the credit card, because a scorecard’s accuracy ratio depends only on the bank’s own default rate.

statement: Monitoring of a scorecard is needed only once the economic cycle turns, because the characteristics and behaviour of a scored population are stable in normal times.
explanation: Populations and their behaviour change over time in any phase of the cycle, so scorecard monitoring has to be continuous.
originalText: Monitoring is needed only once the economic cycle turns, because the characteristics and behaviour of a scored population are stable in normal times.

statement: In risk-based pricing, the probability of take-up is an external market input that itself depends on the price and credit limit offered, while the cost of equity capital is an internal input.
explanation: Risk-based pricing draws on external market data, such as the probability of take-up, which is a function of price and credit limit. It also draws on internal inputs such as the cost of equity capital.
originalText: The probability of take-up is an external market input that itself depends on the price and credit limit offered, while the cost of equity capital is an internal input.

statement: Once the PD of a score band is known, the price can be set from the PD alone, since LGD, EAD and allocated capital are the same for every account.
explanation: PD is only one of the inputs to a risk-based price. LGD, EAD and allocated capital differ across accounts and are priced in as well.

statement: Operating expenses are left out of risk-based pricing, because it prices credit risk only.
explanation: Operating expenses are an explicit input to risk-based pricing, together with take-up probability, PD, LGD, EAD, allocated capital and the cost of equity capital.
originalText: Operating expenses are left out, because risk-based pricing prices credit risk only.

statement: In risk-based pricing, the probability of take-up is an internal input, estimated from the bank's own default history in each score band.
explanation: Take-up is the probability that the customer accepts the offer, an external market input depending on price and credit limit. It is not estimated from default history.
originalText: The probability of take-up is an internal input, estimated from the bank’s own default history in each score band.

statement: Risk-based pricing is now mature in retail banking, and banks' key business objectives are generally well reflected in their pricing strategies.
explanation: Risk-based pricing in retail financial services remains in its infancy, and banks' key business objectives are seldom adequately reflected in their pricing.
originalText: Risk-based pricing is now mature in retail banking, and banks’ key business objectives are generally well reflected in their pricing strategies.

statement: Under risk-based pricing the bank no longer faces a trade-off between growing market share and limiting the rate of bad accounts.
explanation: Pricing is used to balance market share against the rate of bad accounts, so the trade-off remains under risk-based pricing.

statement: Risk-based pricing suits banks only, and nonbanks that extend credit to consumers should avoid it because it does not apply outside banking.
explanation: GARP says risk-based pricing should also be used when nonbanks offer credit. The obstacle is that many nonbanks lack the logistical and operational infrastructure.
originalText: Risk-based pricing suits banks only; nonbanks that extend credit to consumers should avoid it because it does not apply outside banking.

statement: Default spreads give a more granular and more dynamic view of sovereign default risk than ratings, but they are more volatile and can move with liquidity and investor demand for reasons unrelated to default.
explanation: Market spreads differentiate risk more finely than rating agencies, for example by separating two countries with the same rating. They tend to be far more volatile than ratings and can be affected by liquidity and investor demand.
originalText: Spreads give a more granular and more dynamic view of default risk than ratings, but they are more volatile and can move with liquidity and investor demand for reasons unrelated to default.

statement: Default spreads on sovereign bonds are less volatile than credit ratings.
explanation: Market-based default spreads are far more volatile than ratings, which are updated infrequently.
originalText: Default spreads are less volatile than ratings, because they average the views of many investors.
correction: Default spreads on sovereign bonds are more volatile than credit ratings.

statement: Sovereign default spreads can be compared across countries by measuring each country's local currency bond yield against the US Treasury yield.
explanation: Local currency yields embed expected inflation, so they cannot be compared across countries. A default spread needs a default-free bond in the same currency as the bond being assessed.
originalText: The same comparison could be made with the three countries’ local currency bond yields, provided each is measured against the US Treasury yield.

statement: After a credit event such as a failure to pay, a restructuring or a bankruptcy, the CDS seller either buys the reference bonds at par or pays par minus their market price, and the protection is only as good as the seller's own credit standing.
explanation: The seller settles physically by buying the bonds at par, or in cash by paying par minus the market price. The buyer is exposed to the seller's ability to pay.
originalText: After a failure to pay, a restructuring or a bankruptcy, the seller either buys the bonds at par or pays par minus their market price, and the protection is only as good as the seller’s own credit standing.

statement: If a bond's price falls sharply in a liquidity squeeze while the issuer keeps paying, the CDS protection seller must compensate the buyer for the fall.
explanation: A CDS pays out only after a credit event. A price fall without a credit event is not compensated.
originalText: If the bonds’ price falls sharply in a liquidity squeeze while Colombia keeps paying, the protection seller must compensate the manager for the fall.

statement: A CDS protection buyer carries no exposure to the protection seller when the reference entity is a sovereign.
explanation: The protection buyer is exposed to the seller's ability to pay whatever the reference entity is.
originalText: Because the reference entity is a sovereign, the manager carries no exposure to the protection seller.

statement: Under cash settlement of a CDS, the seller pays the full par value and also takes delivery of the bonds.
explanation: Cash settlement pays par minus the market price of the bonds, with no delivery. Physical settlement pays par against delivery of the bonds.
originalText: Under cash settlement the seller pays the full par value of USD 10 million and also takes delivery of the bonds.

statement: A change in a sovereign rating remains an informational event with a price impact when it occurs, and bond markets draw on ratings just as agencies draw on market data, so ratings remain useful alongside spreads.
explanation: Although market measures lead the agencies, it would be a mistake to conclude that sovereign ratings are useless. Bond markets use ratings and rating changes when pricing bonds.
originalText: A rating change is still an informational event with a price impact when it occurs, and bond markets draw on ratings just as agencies draw on market data, so ratings remain useful alongside spreads.

statement: Credit ratings are better predictors of sovereign default than either market default spreads or CDS spreads.
explanation: Market measures adjust faster than ratings, and changes in CDS spreads are emerging as better predictors of default than ratings.
originalText: Ratings are better predictors of default than either market measure, because each rating is set only after a committee review.

statement: Sovereign default spreads are uncorrelated with credit ratings, so the two measures carry unrelated information.
explanation: Default spreads are correlated with both ratings and actual default.
originalText: Default spreads are uncorrelated with ratings, so the two measures carry unrelated information and both should be kept.

statement: Changes in sovereign CDS spreads tend to lead changes in bond yields and ratings, but a spike may reflect counterparty and liquidity risk rather than higher default risk.
explanation: CDS spreads are the most timely signal. Counterparty and liquidity risk, endemic to the CDS market, can move CDS prices in ways that have little to do with default risk.

statement: Evidence shows sovereign CDS spreads to be clearly superior to default spreads on government bonds as a measure of default risk.
explanation: CDS changes provide information, albeit noisy, but there is little to indicate that they are superior to market default spreads obtained from government bonds.
originalText: Sovereign CDS spreads update continuously, and the evidence shows them to be clearly superior to default spreads on government bonds as a measure of default risk.

statement: Default spreads on sovereign bonds tend to widen only after a rating downgrade, so the bond market confirms agency assessments rather than anticipating them.
explanation: The sovereign bond market leads the rating agencies: default spreads usually climb ahead of a downgrade and drop before an upgrade.

statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the buyer deliver bonds with a face value equal to the notional and receive that face value, while cash settlement has the seller pay the notional times one minus the auction value of the cheapest deliverable bond per unit of face value.
explanation: Both routes leave the buyer with about the face value: either cash from the seller, or the face value paid for delivered bonds. Cash settlement pays the loss, notional times (1 minus the recovery value).
originalText: Physical settlement: the buyer delivers bonds with a face value equal to the notional and receives their face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the notional times one minus the auction value of the cheapest deliverable bond per unit of face value.

statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the seller deliver the reference entity's bonds to the buyer at their post-default price, while cash settlement has the seller pay the buyer the market value of the defaulted bonds.
explanation: In physical settlement the buyer delivers the bonds and receives face value. Cash settlement pays the loss (notional times one minus the recovery value), not the recovery value.
originalText: Physical settlement: the seller delivers the reference entity’s bonds to the buyer at their post-default price; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the market value of the defaulted bonds.

statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the reference entity buy back its bonds from the buyer at face value, while cash settlement has the seller pay the buyer the full notional.
explanation: The reference entity is not a party to the CDS. Under physical settlement the seller buys the bonds at face value, and cash settlement pays only the loss, not the full notional.
originalText: Physical settlement: the reference entity buys back its bonds from the buyer at face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the full notional.

statement: When a CDS allowing delivery of several bonds is cash settled through an auction, the auction values the cheapest deliverable bond and the seller pays the notional times one minus that value, so the cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer.
explanation: The buyer may deliver any eligible bond and will choose the cheapest, so the cheapest bond sets the payoff. The delivery option therefore belongs to the buyer and makes protection more valuable.
originalText: The auction values the cheapest deliverable bond, the one trading at 35, so the seller pays 65% of notional; the cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer.

statement: The payoff of a cash-settled CDS is based on the average of the prices of the deliverable bonds, so neither party gains from the choice of bond.
explanation: The payoff is not an average. The cheapest deliverable bond sets it, and the choice of bond is an option held by the protection buyer.
originalText: The payoff is based on the average of the three prices, so neither party gains from the choice of bond.

statement: The payoff of a cash-settled CDS is based on the most expensive deliverable bond, and the choice of bond benefits the protection seller.
explanation: The cheapest deliverable bond sets the payoff, so the option benefits the protection buyer, not the seller.
originalText: The payoff is based on the bond trading at 41, so the seller pays 59% of notional; the choice of bond benefits the protection seller.

statement: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the seller pays the buyer the present value of the difference upfront, and afterwards the buyer pays the fixed coupon until maturity or a credit event.
explanation: Paying a coupon above the market spread overpays the seller, so the seller compensates the buyer upfront. After that the running payment is the standard coupon.
originalText: The seller pays the buyer the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon until maturity or a credit event.

statement: No upfront payment is made on a standard-coupon CDS when the quoted spread is below the coupon, and the buyer simply pays the quoted spread each year.
explanation: An upfront payment is needed whenever the quoted spread and the standard coupon differ, and the running payment is the coupon, not the quoted spread.
originalText: No upfront payment is made because the quoted spread is below the coupon; the buyer pays 60 bp a year.

statement: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the buyer pays the seller the present value of the difference upfront and then pays the coupon.
explanation: When the spread is below the coupon, the seller pays the buyer the upfront amount. The buyer pays upfront only when the quoted spread is above the coupon.
originalText: The buyer pays the seller the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon.
correction: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the seller pays the buyer the present value of the difference upfront and then the buyer pays the coupon.

changes.from: the buyer pays the seller the present value
changes.to: the seller pays the buyer the present value
and then the buyer pays the coupon

statement: The position of a CDS buyer is approximately that of someone long a risk-free bond and short a corporate bond: the buyer gains as the issuer's credit worsens and pays about the credit spread to hold the position.
explanation: A corporate bond plus bought protection is approximately a risk-free bond, so protection is approximately a long risk-free bond plus a short corporate bond.
originalText: A corporate bond plus bought protection is approximately a risk-free bond, so bought protection is approximately a long risk-free bond plus a short corporate bond: the buyer gains as the issuer’s credit worsens and pays about the credit spread to hold the position.

statement: A CDS buyer gains when the reference entity's credit quality improves, as a holder of its bonds would.
explanation: That describes the CDS seller or a bondholder, who is long the credit. The buyer gains when the reference entity's credit worsens.
originalText: The buyer gains when the reference entity’s credit improves, as a holder of its bonds would.
correction: A CDS seller gains when the reference entity's credit quality improves, as a holder of its bonds would.

statement: A CDS buyer pays the risk-free rate and receives the corporate yield, so the position earns the credit spread.
explanation: Earning the credit spread is the seller's side. The CDS buyer pays about the credit spread for protection.
originalText: The buyer pays the risk-free rate and receives the corporate yield, so the position earns the credit spread.

statement: A CDS buyer has no exposure to the reference entity unless it also owns the entity's bonds.
explanation: The buyer's exposure comes from the contract itself, and owning the bonds is not required.
originalText: The statement is false: a CDS buyer has no exposure to the reference entity unless it also owns the entity’s bonds.

statement: In a credit-linked note issued through an SPV, the investor pays the principal upfront and bears the credit risk of the assets sold to the SPV, with no credit linkage to the sponsoring entity.
explanation: Unlike a note issued directly by the originator, an SPV-issued note is linked to the assets sold to the SPV. Its performance depends on those assets, and the note is funded by the investor's principal.

statement: In a total return swap used to finance a bond purchase, the total return receiver retains ownership of the bond, and the spread over the floating rate compensates the receiver for the risk that the payer defaults.
explanation: In this structure the total return payer buys and retains ownership of the bond. The spread over the floating rate compensates the payer for the risk that the receiver defaults.

statement: The buyer of protection in a credit default swap must own bonds of the reference entity, as with an insurance contract.
explanation: Unlike an insurance contract, a CDS does not require the buyer to own the underlying asset. CDS volume on a company can exceed its outstanding debt.
originalText: In a credit default swap, the protection buyer must own bonds of the reference entity, as with an insurance contract, and receives the notional times one minus the auction price after a credit event.

statement: In a synthetic CDO priced with the one-factor Gaussian copula, base correlation is the correlation that prices each individual tranche, while compound correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.
explanation: The definitions are reversed. Compound (tranche) correlation prices an individual tranche, while base correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.
correction: In a synthetic CDO priced with the one-factor Gaussian copula, compound correlation is the correlation that prices each individual tranche, while base correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.

statement: Default correlation is the major reason that risk-neutral default probabilities are greater than real-world default probabilities, because correlated defaults create systematic risk that investors require compensation for.
explanation: Default correlation means credit risk cannot be completely diversified away. Correlated defaults are systematic risk, which is priced into spreads.

statement: Credit contagion, where one company's default triggers the default of another, reduces default correlation.
explanation: Contagion, where one default causes another, is a reason default correlation exists, so it increases default correlation.
originalText: Credit contagion, where one company’s default triggers another’s, reduces default correlation, because the surviving companies take over the defaulted company’s business.
correction: Credit contagion, where one company's default triggers the default of another, increases default correlation.

statement: In a reduced form model, perfectly correlated hazard rates for two companies make it highly likely that both default within the same short period.
explanation: Even perfectly correlated hazard rates leave joint default in a short period unlikely, which is the main weakness of reduced form models for modelling default correlation.

statement: Because default is rare, default correlation can be ignored in a well-diversified portfolio of investment-grade bonds without affecting the tail of the loss distribution.
explanation: Rarity of default does not make correlation negligible. Default correlation drives the tail of the loss distribution, and diversification cannot remove the common component.

statement: Raising the copula correlation lowers the worst case default rate, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.
explanation: Higher correlation raises the worst case default rate, because clustering of defaults makes the bad years worse.
originalText: Raising the copula correlation from 0.1 to 0.2 lowers the WCDR, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.
correction: Raising the copula correlation raises the worst case default rate, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.

statement: In the Gaussian copula credit VaR model, raising the recovery rate lowers the worst case default rate.
explanation: Recovery affects the credit VaR, because each default costs less, but it leaves the worst case default rate unchanged.
originalText: Raising the recovery rate from 60% to 70% lowers the WCDR, because each default then costs less.

statement: With a copula correlation of zero, the worst case default rate at a 99.9% confidence level still exceeds the PD, because the confidence level always adds a tail term.
explanation: With zero correlation the tail term vanishes and the worst case default rate equals the PD, because the law of large numbers removes uncertainty about the default rate.
originalText: With a copula correlation of zero, the WCDR would still exceed the 2% PD, because the 99.9% confidence level always adds a tail term.

statement: An investor in a credit-linked note issued directly by a bank has sold protection on the reference entity in funded form: after a credit event its principal is repaid less the loss, and it is also exposed to the issuing bank's own credit risk.
explanation: The investor pays principal at issue and the coupon spread is its premium for bearing the reference entity's credit risk. Because the issuer holds the cash and repays the note, the investor also bears the issuer's credit risk.
originalText: The insurer has sold protection on Y in funded form: after a credit event its principal is repaid less the loss on Y, and because Bank X issued the note directly the insurer is also exposed to Bank X’s own credit risk.

statement: The investor in a credit-linked note is the protection buyer: if the reference entity suffers a credit event, the issuing bank compensates the investor for the loss.
explanation: The note investor is the protection seller and loses when the reference entity suffers a credit event.
originalText: The insurer is the protection buyer: if Y suffers a credit event, Bank X compensates the insurer for the loss on Y.

statement: Like a seller of CDS protection, a credit-linked note investor pays nothing at inception and pays cash only if the reference entity suffers a credit event.
explanation: That describes an unfunded CDS sale. A credit-linked note is funded, so the investor pays the principal at issue.
originalText: Like a seller of CDS protection, the insurer pays nothing at inception and pays cash only if Y suffers a credit event.

statement: A credit event at the reference entity of a credit-linked note does not reduce the redemption amount, because the coupon spread compensates the investor only for the issuer's own credit risk.
explanation: The redemption amount is reduced by credit losses on the reference entity. That is the credit link of the note.
originalText: Because Bank X holds the insurer’s cash, the coupon spread compensates the insurer for Bank X’s credit risk only, and a credit event at Y would not reduce the redemption amount.

statement: Re-running the valuation of a regular CDS with a different recovery rate, after re-implying the hazard rate from the same quotes, changes its value very little, whereas a binary CDS on the same name is far more sensitive to the recovery assumption.
explanation: When the hazard rate is implied from market spreads, implied PDs scale roughly with 1/(1-R) while the payoff scales with (1-R), so the effects largely offset for a regular CDS. A binary CDS pays a fixed amount, so it does not offset.
originalText: Re-running the valuation of a regular CDS with a 20% recovery rate, re-implying the hazard rate from the same quotes, changes its value very little; a binary CDS on the same name is far more sensitive to the assumption.

statement: Leaving out the accrual payment on default lowers the breakeven spread of a CDS.
explanation: Without the accrual term the denominator of the breakeven spread formula shrinks, so the breakeven spread rises.
originalText: Leaving out the accrual payment on default lowers the breakeven spread, because the buyer is then assumed to pay less.
correction: Leaving out the accrual payment on default raises the breakeven spread of a CDS.

statement: A binary CDS on a name should trade at a lower spread than the regular CDS on the same name, because its payoff is fixed in advance.
explanation: A binary CDS pays the whole notional on default rather than only the loss (1 minus recovery), so it costs more and trades at a higher spread.
originalText: A binary CDS on the same name should trade at a lower spread than the regular CDS, because its payoff is fixed in advance.

statement: In valuing a CDS, the expected premium payments are weighted by the probability of default in each year, and the expected payoff by the probability of survival to each payment date.
explanation: The weights are swapped. Expected premium payments are weighted by survival probabilities, and the expected payoff by default probabilities.
originalText: The expected premium payments are weighted by the probability of default in each year, and the expected payoff by the probability of survival to each payment date.

statement: After inception a CDS is revalued at zero, because its spread is reset to the market level.
explanation: A CDS is worth zero only at inception. Its spread is fixed for the life of the contract, so later changes in the market spread give it a positive or negative value.
originalText: Zero: a CDS is revalued at zero after inception because its spread is reset to the market level.

statement: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche's spread falls and the senior tranche spreads rise, while the index spread is unchanged.
explanation: Each name keeps its hazard rate, so the portfolio's expected loss and the index spread are unchanged. Higher correlation makes both few and many defaults more likely, which helps the equity tranche and hurts the senior tranches.
originalText: The equity tranche becomes less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche’s price for protection falls and the senior tranche spreads rise; the index spread is unchanged.

statement: Raising the copula correlation raises all tranche spreads, because higher correlation raises each company's probability of default.
explanation: Correlation does not change each name's default probability. It redistributes losses between tranches, lowering the equity spread and raising the senior spreads.
originalText: All tranche spreads rise, because higher correlation raises each company’s probability of default.

statement: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche riskier and the senior tranches safer.
explanation: The equity tranche gains from clustering of defaults and the senior tranches lose.
originalText: The equity tranche becomes riskier and the senior tranches safer, because defaults become more frequent in every scenario.
correction: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier.

changes.from: the equity tranche riskier and the senior tranches safer
changes.to: the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier

statement: Raising the copula correlation changes no tranche price, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.
explanation: The expected portfolio loss is unchanged, but correlation changes how losses are distributed across the tranches, so tranche prices do change.
originalText: No tranche price changes, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.

statement: For the equity tranche of a CDO, compound correlation and base correlation coincide, because the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.
explanation: The equity tranche from 0 to its detachment point is both the first tranche and a base tranche, so the two implied correlation measures give the same number.
originalText: The compound correlations form a smile, lowest for the 3 to 6% tranche, while the base correlations rise steadily with the detachment point; the two coincide at 3%, where the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.

statement: To value a non-standard tranche, GARP's preferred approach is to interpolate the PV of expected loss on the 0 to X% tranches across the standard detachment points, take the difference between the two relevant values, and then imply the tranche's compound correlation and breakeven spread.
explanation: Interpolating the expected losses themselves can respect the no-arbitrage condition, whereas interpolating base correlations often violates it. The quantity that carries the economics is interpolated, not the model parameter.
originalText: Interpolate the PV of expected loss on the 0 to $X$% tranche across the standard detachment points to estimate it for 0 to 4% and 0 to 8%; take the difference as the expected loss on the 4 to 8% tranche, then imply its compound correlation and breakeven spread.

statement: Interpolated base correlations always satisfy the no-arbitrage condition on expected losses.
explanation: Interpolating base correlations often violates the condition that the PV of expected loss on the 0 to X% tranche rises with X at a decreasing rate, because base correlation is a nonlinear function of expected loss.
originalText: Interpolate base correlations at 4% and 8% and use them directly, because interpolated base correlations always satisfy the no-arbitrage condition on expected losses.

statement: A non-standard mezzanine tranche has the same risk as the whole portfolio and can be quoted at the index spread.
explanation: The index spread prices protection on the whole portfolio. A mezzanine tranche has a very different risk and its own breakeven spread.
originalText: Quote the index spread for the 4 to 8% tranche, because a tranche straddling two standard tranches has the same risk as the index.

statement: Bank counterparties contribute little to a dealer's CVA because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.
explanation: Banks contribute little CVA because of their good credit quality and collateralisation, not because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.
originalText: Bank counterparties contribute little CVA because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.

statement: With PFE-based credit limits, a soft limit may be breached through market movements without forcing trades to be unwound, whereas a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action.
explanation: GARP says a soft limit may be breached through market movements but not through new transactions, while a hard limit breach requires remedial action. New trades that would breach a limit are refused unless specifically approved.
originalText: A rise in PFE to USD 12 million caused purely by market moves breaches the soft limit but does not by itself force trades to be unwound, whereas a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action.

statement: A proposed trade is compared with the remaining headroom under a credit limit using its standalone PFE, since netting with existing trades is captured only in CVA.
explanation: The incremental PFE (after minus before the trade) is what counts, and it is smaller than the standalone PFE because of portfolio effects such as netting.
originalText: A proposed trade is compared with the remaining headroom using its standalone PFE, since netting with existing trades is captured only in CVA.

statement: PFE-based credit limits typically step up at longer horizons.
explanation: Limits are often reduced over time, because credit quality may deteriorate over long horizons.
originalText: The limits should step up at longer horizons, because exposures on most derivatives grow with maturity.
correction: PFE-based credit limits typically step down at longer horizons.

statement: Because a soft credit limit can be breached by market moves, new trades that take PFE above the soft limit at a future date can be booked without approval.
explanation: A soft limit may be breached by market movements but not by new transactions. New trades that would breach a limit at any future point are refused unless specifically approved.
originalText: Because the soft limit can be breached by market moves, new trades that take PFE above USD 10 million at a future date can be booked without approval.

statement: The exit-price concept in FAS 157 and IFRS 13 points to risk-neutral default probabilities, and Basel III also defines CVA with respect to credit spreads, although Basel III does not permit DVA.
explanation: Accounting and regulation both point to risk-neutral, spread-based CVA, but they conflict on DVA: accounting recognises it and Basel III does not permit it.

statement: Under the actuarial approach, CVA is the cost of a hedging strategy built from CDS spreads and so already uses market-implied default probabilities.
explanation: The hedging-cost view is the risk-neutral approach. The actuarial view is an expected value based on historical default probabilities, with a risk premium.
originalText: Under the actuarial approach, CVA is the cost of a hedging strategy built from CDS spreads, so it already uses market-implied default probabilities.

statement: Regulators generally accept CVA models based on expected loss from historical default rates, provided the risk premium is excluded.
explanation: Regulators state that models based on expected loss or historical calculations that ignore risk premia are not acceptable.

statement: An uncollateralised trade on which a bank makes an upfront payment must be funded, for example by issuing a bond, because the cash flows that repay it arrive later.
explanation: Lenders require compensation for providing that funding, which creates a funding cost. With collateral, the margin offsets the upfront payment and the funding need largely disappears.
originalText: An uncollateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment must be funded, for example by issuing a bond, because the cash flows that repay it arrive later.

statement: A collateralised trade on which a bank makes an upfront payment needs funding just like an uncollateralised one, because margin never offsets an upfront payment.
explanation: In a collateralised trade the margin received offsets the upfront payment, so the funding need disappears.
originalText: A collateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment needs funding just like an uncollateralised one, because margin never offsets an upfront payment.

statement: Receiving government bonds instead of cash as collateral removes all funding and collateral costs, because bonds can always be converted to cash at no cost.
explanation: A repo rate defines the cost of converting bonds into cash, so the collateral type changes the cost but does not remove it.

statement: Funding costs in derivative valuation are fully objective inputs, because the bank can read them from its bond spreads for any maturity it chooses.
explanation: Some funding inputs are subjective, such as the maturity of funding a trade needs and the dividends shareholders will require.
originalText: Funding costs are fully objective inputs, because the bank can read them from its bond spreads for any maturity it chooses.

statement: One party's CVA cost is the other party's DVA benefit, but capital and initial margin costs are costs to both parties with no equal and opposite benefit to the counterparty.
explanation: One party's positive value is the other's negative value, so CVA and DVA mirror each other. Capital and initial margin costs are always present and do not provide an equal and opposite benefit to the counterparties.
originalText: The trainee is right for CVA and DVA, since one party’s CVA cost is the other’s DVA benefit, but wrong for capital and initial margin, which are costs to both parties with no offsetting benefit.

statement: Every xVA cost borne by one party to a swap is an equal and opposite benefit to the other party, including capital and initial margin costs.
explanation: Symmetry holds for CVA and DVA, but capital and initial margin costs are borne by both parties with no offsetting benefit.
originalText: The trainee is right for every term, because one party’s positive value is always the other’s negative value.

statement: CVA and DVA are costs to both parties of a trade.
explanation: DVA is a benefit to the party whose own default risk it reflects. One party's CVA cost is the other party's DVA benefit.
originalText: The trainee is wrong for every term, because CVA and DVA are costs to both parties.

statement: One bank's regulatory capital charge on a trade is released as capital relief at its counterparty.
explanation: Each bank's capital is set by its own regulator on its own exposure, so there is no mirror capital relief at the counterparty.
originalText: The trainee is right for capital, because one bank’s regulatory capital charge is released as capital relief at its counterparty.

statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the funding valuation adjustment (FVA) pairs the valuation as its market component with the funding cost as its cost component.
explanation: Each xVA term combines a market component with a cost component. For FVA these are the valuation (funding position) and the funding cost.
originalText: FVA: the valuation (funding position) as the market component and the funding cost as the cost component.

statement: In GARP's xVA framework, CVA pairs credit exposure as its market component with the institution's funding cost as its cost component.
explanation: CVA pairs credit exposure with the counterparty's default probability. Funding cost is the cost component of FVA.
originalText: CVA: credit exposure as the market component and the institution’s funding cost as the cost component.

statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the margin valuation adjustment (MVA) pairs the initial margin amount as its market component with the cost of capital as its cost component.
explanation: MVA pairs the initial margin amount with the funding cost of that margin. The cost of capital belongs to KVA.
originalText: MVA: the initial margin amount as the market component and the cost of capital as the cost component.

statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the capital valuation adjustment (KVA) pairs the valuation as its market component with the counterparty's default probability as its cost component.
explanation: KVA pairs the capital amount with the cost of capital. The default probability is the cost component of CVA and DVA.
originalText: KVA: the valuation as the market component and the counterparty’s default probability as the cost component.

statement: Since own-default risk is widely seen as a funding benefit, DVA and the funding benefit adjustment (FBA) can overlap, so adding both may double count.
explanation: GARP notes potential overlaps between xVA terms, for example between DVA and FBA. Some costs could also be classed as either FVA or ColVA because collateral must be funded.

statement: Every cost belongs to exactly one xVA term, so the xVA terms can always be added without double counting.
explanation: The definitions of xVA terms overlap, so adding them blindly can double count.
originalText: Every cost belongs to exactly one xVA term, so the terms can always be added without double counting.

statement: In GARP's convention for plotting xVA profiles, benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values.
explanation: The convention is reversed: costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values.
originalText: In GARP’s convention for plotting xVA profiles, benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values.
correction: In GARP's convention for plotting xVA profiles, costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values.

changes.from: benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values
changes.to: costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values

statement: In a CCP default waterfall, the surviving members' initial margin is used before the mutualised default fund.
explanation: Surviving members' initial margin is not part of the loss waterfall, because loss allocation methods do not let a CCP use the initial margin of non-defaulting members. Survivors pay through their default fund contributions.
originalText: The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb nothing, because the surviving members’ initial margin is applied before the mutualised default fund.

statement: Losses allocated to a CCP's mutualised default fund are shared only among the members that held trades with the defaulted member.
explanation: Mutualisation does not depend on having traded with the defaulter. A member can suffer default losses even if it never traded with the defaulted counterparty.
originalText: The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb EUR 270 million, shared only among the members that held trades with the defaulter.

statement: In a trust securitisation arrangement, the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust, and the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator from the assets.
explanation: The originator sells the receivables to a master trust, which deposits them in a grantor trust and receives a beneficial interest. The notes are backed by that beneficial claim.
originalText: In the trust arrangement the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust; the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator.

statement: A company SPV is the usual form in the US market, because US accounting rules are satisfied by a single entity that issues notes directly against its assets.
explanation: The trust is more common in the US market, because a company may not distance the originator enough for accounting purposes. The single-entity company form is the Euromarkets choice.

statement: Choosing the trust form removes the need for a true sale, because the trustee then holds the receivables on behalf of the originator.
explanation: A trust is still an SPV that must buy the assets in a true sale. The trustee represents the investors' interests, not the originator's.

statement: A company SPV cannot be bankruptcy remote, so investors in its notes keep a claim on the originator if the receivables underperform.
explanation: An SPV, whether a trust or a company, is defined as bankruptcy remote from the sponsor.

statement: For a creditor holding a bond, credit risk is the risk that the issuer fails to honor its contractual interest or principal payments, because of inability, unwillingness or delay.
explanation: Credit risk is the loss arising from a counterparty's inability, unwillingness or nontimeliness in honoring its obligation. For a bond this means missed coupon or principal payments.
originalText: The startup fails to honor its contractual interest or principal payments, because of inability, unwillingness or delay.

statement: For a bond investor, credit risk is the risk of losing money because the issuer fails to meet its coupon and principal obligations.
explanation: Credit risk is the possibility of loss from the obligor's failure to honor its payment obligations, which for a bond are the coupons and principal.
originalText: The investor loses money because the bank fails to meet its coupon and principal obligations.

statement: For a bond investor, the risk that the bond's market value falls because interest rates rise is credit risk.
explanation: A price fall caused by rising interest rates is interest rate (market) risk. It occurs even if the issuer pays in full.
originalText: The market value of the bond falls because interest rates rise.
correction: For a bond investor, the risk that the bond's market value falls because interest rates rise is interest rate risk.

statement: The factors most critical in helping creditors assess credit risk are the amount of credit risk (exposure), the probability of counterparty default, and the recovery amount and timing.
explanation: For each credit risk transaction the three fundamental questions are how much can be lost, how likely default is, and how much is recovered, when and at what cost.
originalText: Amount of credit risk, probability of counterparty default, recovery amount and timing.

statement: An investor lending through a peer-to-peer platform bears credit risk, the risk that the borrower fails to repay the loan.
explanation: Lending exposes the lender to loss if the borrower is unable, unwilling or late in repaying, which is credit risk by definition.
originalText: Credit risk that the borrower fails to repay the loan.

statement: A lender's credit risk on a short-term credit line depends most directly on the likelihood that the client fails to repay, judged from its repayment record and current ability to meet its obligations.
explanation: Credit risk is driven by the borrower's probability of failing to pay. Assessing it means estimating the probability of default from repayment history and present capacity to pay.
originalText: The likelihood that the client fails to repay, based on its repayment record and current ability to meet obligations.

statement: A creditor's credit exposure to a borrower increases when the borrower draws on the credit extended, because available credit becomes an outstanding receivable.
explanation: Credit exposure arises for the party that is owed money. A drawdown converts unused credit into an outstanding receivable for the lender.
originalText: Chazz Bank’s credit exposure to Jason increased on January 25, when his purchase drew on the credit extended to him.

statement: A borrower who owes money to a bank is the party exposed to credit risk on that debt.
explanation: The obligor owes the money, so the bank, as creditor, is exposed to the risk of non-payment. A debtor does not bear credit risk on its own borrowing.
originalText: Jason became exposed to credit risk on January 25 because he now owes \$2,500 to the bank.

statement: A lender has no credit risk on a credit line until the borrower misses a payment due date.
explanation: Credit risk exists from the moment credit is extended, because the risk is the possibility of loss and not its realization.
originalText: Chazz Bank has no credit risk until Jason misses the February 15 due date.

statement: A corporation whose liabilities exceed its assets is insolvent, even if it expects to meet its upcoming payments and has not sought court protection.
explanation: Insolvency is a balance-sheet condition (negative equity). It can exist before any payment is missed and before any court filing.
originalText: insolvent.

statement: A corporation is bankrupt as soon as its liabilities exceed its assets.
explanation: Bankruptcy is a legal procedure of seeking court protection. Negative equity alone, which is insolvency, does not trigger it.
originalText: bankrupt.

statement: A corporation is in default as soon as its liabilities exceed its assets, even if no payment obligation has been missed.
explanation: Default requires a failure to meet a contractual obligation. A firm with negative equity that still expects to pay is insolvent but not in default.
originalText: in default.

statement: A company whose liabilities exceed its assets and that has missed scheduled payments is both insolvent and in default, but it is not bankrupt until it files for court protection.
explanation: Insolvency is a balance-sheet condition, default is a failure to meet obligations, and bankruptcy is a court procedure. The company meets only the first two.
originalText: XYZ is both insolvent and in default, but not bankrupt.

statement: A corporation that cannot repay a short-term loan when it falls due is in default, and the default could be due to illiquidity.
explanation: Default is a failure to meet a contractual obligation. A shortfall of current assets against current liabilities makes illiquidity a plausible cause.
originalText: Old Crow defaulted on 1/1/2023, and the default could be due to illiquidity.

statement: A corporation's default on a loan does not by itself make it bankrupt, because bankruptcy requires seeking court protection.
explanation: Default and bankruptcy are distinct. Bankruptcy is a legal procedure that involves a court.
originalText: Old Crow’s default on 1/1/2023 does not by itself make it bankrupt.

statement: A corporation whose total assets exceed its total liabilities is solvent, even if its current assets fall short of its current liabilities.
explanation: Solvency compares total assets with total liabilities. Such a firm is solvent but may be illiquid.
originalText: Old Crow was solvent on 12/31/2022.

statement: Bankruptcy of a corporation is a legal procedure, typically following default, in which the corporation seeks court protection and the court negotiates with management and creditors toward liquidation or reorganization.
explanation: The involvement of a court distinguishes bankruptcy from insolvency and default. The outcome is liquidation or reorganization.
originalText: A legal procedure, typically following default, in which the corporation seeks court protection and the court negotiates with management and creditors toward liquidation or reorganization.

statement: Bankruptcy is a condition in which a corporation's liabilities exceed its assets.
explanation: That describes insolvency, a balance-sheet state. Bankruptcy is a legal process.
originalText: A condition in which the corporation’s liabilities exceed its assets.

statement: Bankruptcy is a failure to meet a contractual obligation, such as a missed payment.
explanation: That describes default. Default usually precedes bankruptcy but is not the same thing.
originalText: A failure to meet a contractual obligation, such as a missed payment.

statement: Bankruptcy is an informal, out-of-court agreement between a debtor and its creditors to restructure its debt.
explanation: An out-of-court restructuring involves no court, while bankruptcy is a legal procedure involving a court.
originalText: An informal, out‑of‑court agreement between the debtor and its creditors to restructure its debt.

statement: In non-recourse receivables financing, the finance company's principal credit exposure is the risk that the account debtors fail to pay their invoices on time or at all.
explanation: With non-recourse terms the finance company cannot claw back losses from the manufacturer, so repayment depends on the buyers paying their invoices.
originalText: Receivables; the risk that the manufacturer’s customers (the account debtors) fail to pay their invoices on time or at all

statement: In non-recourse receivables financing, the finance company's principal credit exposure is the deterioration of the financial condition of the manufacturer that sold it the receivables.
explanation: With non-recourse terms the manufacturer's solvency is not the main source of loss. The credit risk sits with the account debtors who owe the invoices.
originalText: Lending to the manufacturer only; the risk that the manufacturer’s own financial condition deteriorates

statement: Credit risk arises not only from lending but also from leases, receivables, prepayments, claims on assets held by others such as deposits, contingent claims such as insurance policies, and derivatives.
explanation: A credit sale creates a receivable, a prepayment depends on the supplier delivering, a deposit is a claim on the bank, and an insurance policy is a contingent claim on the insurer.
originalText: All four: the insurance policy, the prepayment, the credit sales and the bank deposit

statement: Credit risk arises only from lending money.
explanation: Credit risk also arises from receivables, prepayments, deposits, contingent claims such as insurance, leases and derivatives.
originalText: None of them; credit risk arises only from lending money

statement: A lender under a repurchase agreement still bears credit risk, because if the client defaults it may not be able to sell the collateral bonds to cover the full amount lent.
explanation: Collateral reduces but does not remove credit risk, because the bonds' liquidation value is uncertain at the time of default.
originalText: credit risk because if the client defaults, the bank may not be able to sell the bonds to cover the full amount of the repurchase agreement.

statement: A repurchase agreement carries no credit risk for the lender if the repurchase agreement matures before the collateral bonds do.
explanation: A maturity mismatch is irrelevant to whether exposure exists. The lender is exposed throughout the life of the agreement.
originalText: no credit risk because the repurchase agreement matures before the bonds.

statement: A repurchase agreement with an investment grade counterparty carries no credit risk, because counterparty default is unlikely.
explanation: Investment grade lowers the probability of default but does not make it zero.
originalText: no credit risk because the client is rated investment grade; therefore, counterparty default is unlikely.

statement: A repurchase agreement carries no credit risk when the notional value of the collateral bonds exceeds the amount lent.
explanation: Notional (face) value is not realizable market value. A small cushion can be eroded by price falls or illiquidity.
originalText: no credit risk because the notional value of the bonds exceeds the value of the repurchase agreement.
